A one-hour recording

Measured at 2.17.0 (2026-10-25) on one 60-minute 1080p30 H.264 file (4.3 GB, AAC mono 48 kHz, synthetic testsrc2 picture and a tone). The machine was a 4-vCPU Xeon at 2.1 GHz with FFmpeg 6.1.1 on Linux, and each tool ran alone. The analysis rows read the whole hour (silence.py, scenes.py and check.py report 3600 s). The edit and export rows used 10-minute segments cut from it with stream copy, and the last row is the whole hour.

Step Wall time Note
probe.py 0.3 s
silence.py --list 14 s one audio decode
loudness.py --measure-only 66 s
look.py (contact sheet) 97 s
scenes.py 241 s
check.py --platform youtube --content 308 s the rows, dropouts included, cover the full hour
cut.py, a 10-minute stream-copy segment 2.4–4.4 s no re-encode
join.py, two 10-minute segments 624 s join.py re-encodes by default, so it can crossfade and conform (--copy does not, for clips that match)
export.py --preset youtube, a 10-minute segment 514 s about 1.2× real time at the default medium preset
export.py --preset youtube --fast, the same segment 162 s about 3.7× real time at veryfast
export.py --preset youtube, the whole hour killed at 1802 s kind: timeout at the default --timeout of 1800 s (below)

A full-length re-encode of an hour does not fit in the default --timeout. The limit is 1800 s per ffmpeg call. On this machine export.py --preset youtube on the whole hour was killed at 1802 s with kind: timeout (exit 124), and nothing was written. At the 10-minute segment's rate it would have needed about 50 minutes. A whole-hour join.py would land at the limit. The error message names the fix. For a long master, pass --timeout 0 (no limit) or a larger value, or --fast, which at the measured rate takes about 16 minutes for the hour. Analysis tools and stream-copy cuts stay far below the limit.

Plan a long edit or batch

  1. Probe the master and make one lightweight copy for review with python3 scripts/proxy.py master.mp4 --width 640 -o review.mp4. Use the master for the final cut and check the chosen boundaries on its timeline.
  2. Run whole-file analysis once and save the results. For example, python3 scripts/silence.py master.mp4 --list --json > silence.json lists the ranges to review. Pass the chosen ranges to cut.py --segments. When the delivery uses only selected material, trim before reframing, adding captions, or applying effects.
  3. Time a representative segment at the final resolution, codec, and quality to set the export timeout. Watch peak memory across the tool and its FFmpeg children. For a batch, start with --jobs 1 and increase to --jobs 2 on the same sample only if throughput improves and the workstation has memory headroom. Each concurrent encode has its own decoder, filter buffers, and encoder threads. A parallel batch shares one timeout across its items.

An agent-agnostic marketplace at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json points at the same release-built plugin branch directory as the Claude marketplace. Codex can add it without a sparse checkout of .claude-plugin (checked against Codex CLI 0.171.0):

codex plugin marketplace add kajisho5/ffmpeg-skill
codex plugin add ffmpeg-skill@ffmpeg-skill

Those hosts find a plugin's skill only at skills/ffmpeg-skill/SKILL.md, a generated copy of the root SKILL.md (.github/scripts/build_plugin_skill.py; a test fails when it is stale). A Cursor plugin manifest (.cursor-plugin/plugin.json) is in the repository for the Cursor Marketplace; it follows Cursor's reference and has not been through their review yet. The Codex manifest is .codex-plugin/plugin.json; Claude and Cursor manifests are unchanged.

The plugin namespaces the skill as ffmpeg-skill:ffmpeg-skill. The manifests are .claude-plugin/plugin.json, whose version follows every release automatically, and .claude-plugin/marketplace.json (and the matching .agents/plugins/marketplace.json), which name the ffmpeg-skill/ directory of the plugin branch: the 2.7 MB a running skill reads, rebuilt by every release, and not the 28 MB repository. --sparse .claude-plugin keeps the Claude marketplace checkout small as well (measured at 3.4.0: 1.1 MB instead of 50 MB in Claude Code 2.1.322, 2.2 MB instead of 66 MB in Codex 0.167); without it the install is the same and only that checkout is larger. A git-subdir source needs Claude Code 2.1.69 or later (2.1.288 or later where git is older than 2.39, such as Ubuntu 22.04, by Claude Code's changelog; not run here); on anything older, update Claude Code or use npx ffmpeg-skill. Before 2.17.1 the README's one-line claude plugin install kajisho5/ffmpeg-skill could not work, because there was no marketplace file.

Gemini CLI is the exception to that size: gemini extensions install with a repository URL clones the default branch, so that install is the whole repository (about 28 MB: tests, evals, the demo gallery), not the plugin branch. It works, and it is the only route here that copies more than the skill needs.

Without Node: clone this repository and copy SKILL.md, package.json, LICENSE, scripts/, templates/, mcp/, references/ and the one file docs/contract.md into your agent's skills directory. That is the set npx ffmpeg-skill installs, plus references/process-pitfalls.md, a maintainer diary the package leaves out. Do not copy the rest of docs/: in a clone it is about 14 MB of demo-gallery GIFs that no tool reads. Without templates/ no --template renders, and without package.json the contract reports its version as unknown.

After installing:

npx ffmpeg-skill doctor           # every required FFmpeg component present?
npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json  # what the agent framework will see

FFmpeg itself:

OS Command
macOS brew install ffmpeg-full, then put it on PATH (below). The plain ffmpeg formula lacks the subtitles, drawtext and zscale filters
Ubuntu / Debian sudo apt install ffmpeg
Windows winget install Gyan.FFmpeg

On macOS, ffmpeg-full is keg-only: Homebrew installs it without linking it, so after brew install ffmpeg-full the ffmpeg on PATH is still the lean ffmpeg formula (often present as a dependency of another formula), or no ffmpeg at all. If the ffmpeg on PATH is Homebrew's lean formula, the skill uses the ffmpeg-full of the same Homebrew prefix by itself (ffmpeg and ffprobe both, from opt/ffmpeg-full/bin; doctor says so, and doctor --json gives ffmpeg_path / ffmpeg_source); any other ffmpeg on PATH (a tap build, MacPorts, a static download) is used as it is. With no ffmpeg on PATH at all, or to make the whole shell use it, do one of two things:

  • Put it first on PATH. Add export PATH="$(brew --prefix ffmpeg-full)/bin:$PATH" to your shell profile. brew --prefix ffmpeg-full is the stable opt/ path, so this survives upgrades, but it only reaches processes started from a shell that read the profile.
  • Link it over the lean formula: brew unlink ffmpeg 2>/dev/null; brew link --overwrite --force ffmpeg-full. Every process finds this one, but brew doctor warns about a linked keg-only formula, and an upgrade of the lean ffmpeg has been seen to link the lean build back on top without a message. After upgrading, check that command -v ffmpeg still resolves into ffmpeg-full, and re-run the link if it doesn't.

Updating

Releases are frequent (often several a week). Use the update method that matches how you installed the skill.

grep '"version"' ~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/package.json   # the version installed (Cursor: ~/.cursor/skills, Codex: ~/.agents/skills)
npm view ffmpeg-skill version                                  # the latest release
npx ffmpeg-skill@latest setup                                   # install or refresh for each detected agent home; if FFmpeg is missing, may run the system package manager
npx ffmpeg-skill@latest setup --no-ffmpeg                       # same without a package manager; still runs doctor (nonzero if FFmpeg is missing)
npx ffmpeg-skill@latest --cursor                                # one home agent without setup (also --claude, --codex); skips doctor
npx ffmpeg-skill@latest --project                               # run from the same project directory
npx ffmpeg-skill@latest --dir ./my-skills                        # use the same parent directory as before

For plugin and extension installs:

Host Update Uninstall
Claude Code Run claude plugin marketplace update ffmpeg-skill, then claude plugin update ffmpeg-skill@ffmpeg-skill. Restart Claude Code to apply the update. Run claude plugin uninstall ffmpeg-skill@ffmpeg-skill.
Codex CLI On 0.167.0, run codex plugin marketplace upgrade ffmpeg-skill. When the configured marketplace yields an upgraded root, Codex attempts to refresh the cache for the existing configured plugin installation. Run codex plugin remove ffmpeg-skill@ffmpeg-skill.
Gemini CLI Run gemini extensions update ffmpeg-skill to pull changes from the source. Run gemini extensions uninstall ffmpeg-skill. Restart the Gemini CLI session after either change.

For a Claude Code project or local install, add the matching --scope project or --scope local to both claude plugin update and claude plugin uninstall. Before Claude Code 2.1.281, plugin update defaults to user scope when the flag is omitted.

On Codex CLI 0.167.0, if the marketplace is already current but the cached plugin is still old, rerun codex plugin add ffmpeg-skill@ffmpeg-skill after the release reaches the plugin branch. This refreshes the cache without a separate uninstall and sets the plugin to enabled in your Codex user config.

A copy made by hand (see "Without Node" above) is updated by copying the same files again from a newer clone or release, replacing the old ones.

npx ffmpeg-skill@4.1.3 installs that exact version, for a setup that should not move. What changed between two versions is in CHANGELOG.md, one short section per release. Within 4.x an update does not break a call to one of the 12 stable tools (see Stability).

Troubleshooting an installed copy

Run these checks in the environment that runs the skill, not just in a separate shell. Run the first command from the directory that holds the installed copy's scripts/: the skill's own directory for a copy made by npx ffmpeg-skill, a Claude Code plugin or a copy by hand, and the plugin's top directory (the one that contains skills/) for the Codex plugin:

python3 scripts/_contract.py doctor --json  # from the directory that holds scripts/
npx ffmpeg-skill doctor --json              # checks the invoked npm package, not a plugin copy
  • It works in my terminal but not in my agent. Compare ffmpeg_path and ffprobe_path against the binaries seen by the agent (a copy older than 3.13.0 does not report them: update it first, see Updating). Use both binaries from the same build, and restart the host after changing the PATH it inherits. If the direct Python command fails, check python3 --version (3.10 or newer); on Windows, use python or py -3 if python3 is unavailable.
  • A specific tool won't run. In the installed copy's report, look under tools (for example, tools.stabilize) for that tool's usable status and any fix message. See Quick start for how to interpret the overall status.
  • The agent still uses an older version. Use the installed copy's version in the report, then follow Updating for that installation route. A newer version reported by the npm command doesn't establish that the agent's own copy was updated.

Requirements

  • FFmpeg 6.1+ (3.0.0 removed 5.x; an older build is refused). Required by at least one tool (so doctor's ok needs them all): libx264, aac, and the drawtext, subtitles (libass), loudnorm, xfade, acrossfade, amix, overlay, scdet, silencedetect, cropdetect, tile, tpad, boxblur, hqdn3d, yadif, reverse, rotate, showwaves, v360, xstack and vidstabdetect/vidstabtransform (libvidstab, stabilize.py only) filters; doctor --json lists them as capabilities.required. Needed only by the flags that use them: libx265, prores_ks, libzimg / zscale, libmp3lame, libopus, libvorbis, the ass filter. doctor tells you which are present. The apt and gyan.dev builds carry all of them; some Homebrew bottles lack libass / libfreetype / libzimg, which doctor reports as missing.
  • Python 3.10+, standard library only (3.0.0 removed 3.9)
  • Node 16+ only for the npx installer

doctor's own introspection calls (ffmpeg -filters/-encoders/-bsfs/-version) time out after 10s and report failed rather than hanging forever — those are meant to be fast. Every tool's actual media-processing ffmpeg invocation (cut, fit, caption, ...) runs under --timeout (default 1800 s, FFMPEG_SKILL_TIMEOUT, 0 = none): past the limit the process is killed, its partial output removed, and the failure reported as kind: timeout (exit 124) — a legitimately long --accurate re-encode should raise the limit rather than run unbounded. -nostdin is always passed, so a hung ffmpeg process waiting on stdin cannot happen.

Stability

4.x splits the promise by tool: the 12 core tools (stability: stable in contract --json) keep every tool name, CLI argument, JSON output key and exit code working until 5.0, as every tool did in 3.x; the other 29 (beta) may drop or rename an argument or an output key in a minor release after one minor of notice in deprecated. The full list of what is promised and what is not, and the three-step deprecation policy, is in docs/contract.md. It is enforced by a test that pins every tool's argument names against a snapshot, so a breaking change fails CI instead of slipping into a patch. Releases are batched: related fixes and features ship together as one version rather than one version per merged pull request, so a dependent project sees fewer, larger steps. Pin a tagged version, not main. 2.0.0 made the five changes announced since 1.10.0 -- --crf removed in favour of --quality (except on export.py, whose preset chooses the encoder), an existing output refused without --overwrite, probe's hdr narrowed to a real HDR signal, json/progress out of the MCP schema, the result_v2 preview withdrawn -- listed with what to change in docs/contract.md and under removed in contract --json. 3.0.0 is the second break: it removed FFmpeg 5.x and Python 3.9 (announced in 2.14.0 and 2.10.9), made cut.py keep an .mp4/.mov copy's edit list, keep an SDR HEVC source HEVC and use --vfr-guard sampled by default (--no-edit-list, --no-keep-hevc and --vfr-guard average restore 2.x), and changed what cut.py's precision (now the least exact segment's) and keyframe_snapped (now equal to start_snapped) mean (contract_version 2.0) -- see docs/contract.md. 4.0.0 is the third: it split the promise by tool (above), made export.py exit non-zero when a video delivery misses a required property, made fit.py --duration ask for --method before a retime beyond 1.15x, turned on content checks in the delivery templates, and gave unusable inputs their own error.reason -- see docs/contract.md.

Development

npm test                      # tests/run_parallel.py (test_all.py's end-to-end modules, sharded across the cores) + tests/test_contract.py
python3 tests/test_picture.py # one tool group on its own (analysis, editing, cut_copy, audio, picture, delivery, orchestration, accel, asr)
npm run release-check         # pack, install, contract from the installed copy, MCP == contract, doctor, tests, contract evals
npm run demo                  # python3 demos/build.py: the clips in demos/footage -> every before/after demo + docs/demos/*.gif
npm run demo:pipeline         # examples/make_demo.sh: the older single end-to-end run, one clip through 13 of the 41 scripts
python3 evals/run.py --list   # agent eval prompts (see evals/); regex-only grading, runnable from any agent harness -- see evals/README.md "Running this from Cursor, Codex, or another harness"
node bin/install.js --dir /tmp/skills   # try the installer without touching ~/.claude

CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs on every pull request and on pushes to main, on Ubuntu (FFmpeg 6.1 with Python 3.10 on 24.04, FFmpeg 8.0.1 with Python 3.13 on 26.04), macOS (Homebrew FFmpeg 8.x) and Windows (gyan.dev FFmpeg 9.x), plus a Linux job on FFmpeg 7.1 (Debian trixie container), and uploads each runner's FFmpeg listings as an artifact.

tests/test_contract.py runs on all three OSes, but some of its tests put a fake ffmpeg or ffprobe (a #!/bin/sh script on a PATH shim) in front of the real one — to record every call under --dry-run, to force specific FFmpeg 6/7/8/9 fixture layouts through doctor's parser, to report an old version, to hang or fail on cue — or need what Windows does not have or does differently (SIGTERM, unprivileged symlinks, a line break or a backslash in a file name). Those tests, among them test_dry_run_never_runs_ffmpeg_and_writes_nothing and the whole DoctorDetectionTests class, skip there (skipIf, or skipTest inside the test) and show as skipped, not silently absent, in the Windows job's log; grep -n 'os.name == "nt"\|platform.system() == "Windows"' tests/test_contract.py finds their conditions, among the suite's other platform branches. The rest — contract schema, reencodes_*, doctor.tools, MCP derivation, and the tools exercised through the contract, including cut.py's provenance fields — runs against the real Windows ffmpeg on every PR. See references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md for this and other per-OS behaviour differences already diagnosed, before spending a CI cycle re-diagnosing a platform-only failure.

Releasing is fully automated end to end, including the version number itself — a PR never needs to touch package.json or the version in docs/contract.md. CHANGELOG.md is different: the release writes the version heading and one line per merged PR, but a feat PR writes its own notes as a fragment file under changelog.d/ (CONTRIBUTING.md, changelog.d/README.md), which the release folds into the new section, and a PR that closes an issue must name that issue in CHANGELOG.md or test_changelog_mentions_every_closed_issue_since_last_tag fails. Once a PR merges to main, .github/workflows/release.yml takes it from there: if nobody bumped the version by hand, it resolves the next version with .github/scripts/resolve_version.py. What that script reads, its rules, their exceptions and the incidents behind them are written once, in its docstring, and test_release_version_resolver_rules and test_release_version_resolver_does_not_depend_on_a_pr_title pin them; they are not restated here. Most PRs don't need a label added by hand: release-drafter.yml's autolabel job applies one automatically from the PR's title/changed files (Fix ... → fix, Add .../feat ... → feature, docs/.md/.github//build(deps) changes → chore) as soon as it's opened — add a label yourself only to override that. A major version is never chosen automatically: no label rule produces major, and the workflow refuses to auto-bump across a major boundary even if someone applies that label — a real major release is a deliberate package.json bump in a PR, which the manual path below already handles. It bumps package.json, .claude-plugin/plugin.json, docs/contract.md and docs/roadmap.md's released-version sentence, writes a CHANGELOG.md section listing those PRs (and any issues they closed), and pushes that commit to main itself. If another PR merged while the bump was being prepared, the push is refused and that run releases nothing: the newer merge's own run, queued behind it, starts from main's tip and releases both (the bump is never rebased onto a merge it did not read). After the tag it also asks pages.yml to rebuild the site, because the bump commit carries [skip ci] and would otherwise leave the site on the previous version. Either way — auto-bumped or hand-bumped in the PR — it then creates the vX.Y.Z tag, publishes a GitHub Release with notes extracted from CHANGELOG.md's matching section, and publishes the package to npm. A PR that still wants to write its own version bump and CHANGELOG.md prose (e.g. to explain the "why" of a release by hand) can — the automation only fills in when nobody made that call already. A push to main with nothing new to release creates no tag, Release or npm publish; its MCP Registry step still asks npm and the registry about server.json's version and publishes the entry only when npm has that version and the registry does not, which is how a later run finishes an entry an earlier one failed to publish. npm publishing needs an NPM_TOKEN repo secret (an npm access token with publish rights on this package) — without it the tag and GitHub Release still happen, only the npm step is skipped. A repo that depends on this one (an editing skill, an agent) should pin an ffmpeg-skill version by tag or npm version, not by tracking main — a merged-but-not-yet-released commit on main can be ahead of the last published npm version for the few minutes between merge and this workflow completing.

A version that was tagged but never reached npm (the npm step failed; a re-run of that release sees the tag and skips the publish) is finished by dispatching the same workflow on its tag: gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f version=X.Y.Z. That runs only the workflow's recover job. It refuses a version that is not X.Y.Z, has no tag, or that npm already has, and a run whose commit is not the tagged one: the npm provenance attestation names the run's commit, so it must be the commit the package is built from. It publishes with --provenance under the latest dist-tag when the version is above every stable (non-prerelease) version npm has, and under backport otherwise, so latest never moves back. Then it publishes the plugin branch when no commit there is for this version and the branch's tip is older, and the MCP Registry entry when the registry does not list the version (never for a backport). The GitHub Release is left as it is. A tag cut before the job was added (#448; every tag up to v3.6.3) has no recover job at its commit and cannot be recovered this way.

Contributing a change: see CONTRIBUTING.md.

Docs
docs/use-cases/ six requests end to end: what you say, the commands, the result, what to check
README.ja.md this README in Japanese
CONTRIBUTING.md scope, dev setup, tests, PR expectations
docs/roadmap.md the release history from 1.8.0, one theme per minor, each marked shipped + evaluated, shipped with eval pending, or planned; and what 2.0.0 then removes
docs/design-decisions.md behaviours that look like bugs but are decisions, with rationale and the pinning test; read before filing a bug
CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md Contributor Covenant 2.1; reports go through the SECURITY.md channel
SECURITY.md how to report a vulnerability privately
SKILL.md what the agent reads: workflow, request → tool map, audio-only rules, report format, pitfalls
references/scripts.md per-flag reference for every tool
references/scripts.md § Verdict thresholds every number behind verified and check.py's rows (tolerances, silence levels, per-platform loudness and length), each with the constant or flag it comes from
references/devices.md real-device notes (iPhone HDR, GoPro, DJI, screen recordings)
references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md per-OS ffmpeg/CI behaviour differences already diagnosed once — read before re-diagnosing a Windows/macOS-only test failure
references/process-pitfalls.md process mistakes already made once (breaking a pinned test by narrowing a capability list, retrying a git/GitHub operation this environment can't do, re-designing a fixture instead of recognising a real platform difference) — a living record, add to it whenever one recurs
docs/contract.md the execution contract field by field, MCP relationship, how a planner consumes it
examples/README.md natural-language requests and the commands behind them, brand.json, project.json, batch recipes
tests/fixtures/README.md captured and constructed FFmpeg listings, which is which
CHANGELOG.md what changed in each release

Support

If this skill saves you time, you can help keep it maintained through GitHub Sponsors. Issues and pull requests are just as welcome.

License

MIT

ffmpeg-skill runs your FFmpeg build as a separate executable. FFmpeg has its own license. Its LGPL builds can include encoders such as SVT-AV1 or VideoToolbox when available. Builds with GPL components such as libx264, libx265 or libvidstab use GPL terms. That affects the default x264/x265 encoding paths and the vid.stab filters used by stabilize.py. FFmpeg labels builds configured with --enable-nonfree as non-redistributable. doctor displays the license reported by the selected executable. See FFmpeg's license and distribution information.

item.title: anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins
item.description:
Open source repository of plugins primarily intended for knowledge workers to use in Claude Cowork

Knowledge Work Plugins

Plugins that turn Claude into a specialist for your role, team, and company. Built for Claude Cowork, also compatible with Claude Code.

Why Plugins

Cowork lets you set the goal and Claude delivers finished, professional work. Plugins let you go further: tell Claude how you like work done, which tools and data to pull from, how to handle critical workflows, and what slash commands to expose — so your team gets better and more consistent outcomes.

Each plugin bundles the skills, connectors, slash commands, and sub-agents for a specific job function. Out of the box, they give Claude a strong starting point for helping anyone in that role. The real power comes when you customize them for your company — your tools, your terminology, your processes — so Claude works like it was built for your team.

Plugin Marketplace

We're open-sourcing 11 plugins built and inspired by our own work:

Plugin How it helps Connectors
productivity Manage tasks, calendars, daily workflows, and personal context so you spend less time repeating yourself. Slack, Notion, Asana, Linear, Jira, Monday, ClickUp, Microsoft 365
sales Research prospects, prep for calls, review your pipeline, draft outreach, and build competitive battlecards. Slack, HubSpot, Close, Clay, ZoomInfo, Notion, Jira, Fireflies, Microsoft 365
customer-support Triage tickets, draft responses, package escalations, research customer context, and turn resolved issues into knowledge base articles. Slack, Intercom, HubSpot, Guru, Jira, Notion, Microsoft 365
product-management Write specs, plan roadmaps, synthesize user research, keep stakeholders updated, and track the competitive landscape. Slack, Linear, Asana, Monday, ClickUp, Jira, Notion, Figma, Amplitude, Pendo, Intercom, Fireflies
marketing Draft content, plan campaigns, enforce brand voice, brief on competitors, and report on performance across channels. Slack, Canva, Figma, HubSpot, Amplitude, Notion, Ahrefs, SimilarWeb, Klaviyo
legal Review contracts, triage NDAs, navigate compliance, assess risk, prep for meetings, and draft templated responses. Slack, Box, Egnyte, Jira, Microsoft 365
finance Prep journal entries, reconcile accounts, generate financial statements, analyze variances, manage close, and support audits. Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Slack, Microsoft 365
data Query, visualize, and interpret datasets — write SQL, run statistical analysis, build dashboards, and validate your work before sharing. Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Definite, Hex, Amplitude, Jira
enterprise-search Find anything across email, chat, docs, and wikis — one query across all your company's tools. Slack, Notion, Guru, Jira, Asana, Microsoft 365
bio-research Connect to preclinical research tools and databases (literature search, genomics analysis, target prioritization) to accelerate early-stage life sciences R&D. PubMed, BioRender, bioRxiv, ClinicalTrials.gov, ChEMBL, Synapse, Wiley, Owkin, Open Targets, Benchling
cowork-plugin-management Create new plugins or customize existing ones for your organization's specific tools and workflows. —

Install these directly from Cowork, browse the full collection here on GitHub, or build your own.

Getting Started

Cowork

Install plugins from claude.com/plugins.

Claude Code

# Add the marketplace first
claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins

# Then install a specific plugin
claude plugin install sales@knowledge-work-plugins

Once installed, plugins activate automatically. Skills fire when relevant, and slash commands are available in your session (e.g., /sales:call-prep, /data:write-query).

How Plugins Work

Every plugin follows the same structure:

plugin-name/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json   # Manifest
├── .mcp.json                    # Tool connections
├── commands/                    # Slash commands you invoke explicitly
└── skills/                      # Domain knowledge Claude draws on automatically
  • Skills encode the domain expertise, best practices, and step-by-step workflows Claude needs to give you useful help. Claude draws on them automatically when relevant.
  • Commands are explicit actions you trigger (e.g., /finance:reconciliation, /product-management:write-spec).
  • Connectors wire Claude to the external tools your role depends on — CRMs, project trackers, data warehouses, design tools, and more — via MCP servers.

Every component is file-based — markdown and JSON, no code, no infrastructure, no build steps.

Making Them Yours

These plugins are generic starting points. They become much more useful when you customize them for how your company actually works:

  • Swap connectors — Edit .mcp.json to point at your specific tool stack.
  • Add company context — Drop your terminology, org structure, and processes into skill files so Claude understands your world.
  • Adjust workflows — Modify skill instructions to match how your team actually does things, not how a textbook says to.
  • Build new plugins — Use the cowork-plugin-management plugin or follow the structure above to create plugins for roles and workflows we haven't covered yet.

As your team builds and shares plugins, Claude becomes a cross-functional expert. The context you define gets baked into every relevant interaction, so leaders and admins can spend less time enforcing processes and more time improving them.

Contributing

Plugins are just markdown files. Fork the repo, make your changes, and submit a PR.

item.title: TauricResearch/TradingAgents
item.description:
TradingAgents: Towards Agentic Finance Research

https://tauric.ai

English | Deutsch | Español | français | 日本語 | 한국어 | Português | Русский | 中文

TradingAgents: Towards Agentic Finance Research

Quick start

1. Get an API key

  • Sign up at Tauric Research.
  • Create your Tauric API key.

2. Install

curl -fsSL https://tauric.ai/tradingagents/install.sh | sh

Or with npm: npm i -g @tauric/tradingagents

3. Run

tradingagents

Start your agentic finance research with Tauric!

Models

Provider Needs
Tauric AI Tauric API key
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, OpenRouter their API key
Self-hosted models (vLLM, Ollama) its address and model
AI subscriptions (ChatGPT) tradingagents login chatgpt

With another provider, /login adds a Tauric API key for filings, statements and news. See docs/models.md.

Usage

Type a question and press Enter. Every figure in the answer is marked with its source, and a numbered list of sources follows.

Command Does
/ Open the commands
/model Choose the model and how hard it reasons
/resume Resume an earlier session
/export Save the last answer as a PDF report, or the session as Markdown
/copy Copy the last answer
/help List every command and key

Shift+Tab switches to plan mode, where the agent proposes a research plan first.

Architecture

Agents and skills

The main agent plans the research, reads what the question needs with its data tools, and works the numbers with its compute tools. For depth, it briefs specialist agents, each in its own context:

Agent Covers
Equity Research a company's statements, filings, estimates, valuation, ownership and news
Macro Strategy growth, inflation, rates and the yield curve, credit, sectors, cross-asset moves
Quant Research returns, volatility, drawdowns, correlation and beta, technical indicators
Risk Analysis what could make a position lose, and what would show it early

For a known kind of research it follows a skill:

Area Skills
Companies company snapshot, earnings preview and review, filing review, full analysis
Valuation DCF, relative valuation, scenario analysis
Markets macro outlook, market brief, performance comparison, sector review, technical analysis
Risk portfolio review, risk assessment, thesis review

You can add your own agents and skills as Markdown files (docs/usage.md). TradingAgents researches and answers; it does not place trades.

Documentation

  • Install: the installer, npm, release files and updates.
  • Usage: the terminal, one-off questions, sessions, agents and skills, sources, sync and limits.
  • Models: providers, keys, reasoning and OpenAI-compatible servers.
  • Configuration: files and environment variables.

To report an issue or open a pull request, see CONTRIBUTING.md; to report a security problem, SECURITY.md.

Citation

@article{xiao2024tradingagents,
  title={TradingAgents: Multi-agents LLM financial trading framework},
  author={Xiao, Yijia and Sun, Edward and Luo, Di and Wang, Wei},
  journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2412.20138},
  year={2024}
}

License

Apache-2.0. See LICENSE.

item.title: NVIDIA/SkillSpector
item.description:
Security scanner for AI agent skills. Detect vulnerabilities, malicious patterns, security risks, prompt injection, data exfiltration, and supply-chain risks in Claude Code, Codex, and MCP skills before you install them.

https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/scanning-agent-skills

SkillSpector

Security scanner for AI agent skills. Detect vulnerabilities, malicious patterns, and security risks before installing agent skills.

Overview

AI agent skills (used by Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, etc.) execute with implicit trust and minimal vetting. In the 31,132-skill analyzed subset of the research dataset, 26.1% of skills contain vulnerabilities and 5.2% show likely malicious intent.

SkillSpector helps you answer: "Is this skill safe to install?"

SkillSpector is part of the NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline, which scans, evaluates, and signs agent skills before publication. Skills that pass are published to the NVIDIA skills catalog.

Documentation

  • Scan agent skills before installation — Hosted guide: when to scan, how to read a report, and how to gate installs.
  • Development guide — Architecture, package layout, and how to extend the analyzer pipeline.
  • Security policy — Report suspected vulnerabilities privately to NVIDIA PSIRT.
  • Analysis resource bounds — Fail-closed bundle, parser, nested-artifact, ledger, and finding ceilings.
  • Pi extension — Install SkillSpector as a Pi tool for scanning skills from inside agent sessions.
  • OpenCode extension — Install SkillSpector as an OpenCode tool and /skillspector command for scanning skills from inside agent sessions.
  • LLM analyzer base guide — How to build LLM-powered analyzer nodes on top of LLMAnalyzerBase.
  • Dependency source redirection — How SC10 findings flag a skill that changes where its packages are fetched from.
  • Live vulnerability lookups (SC4) — How SC4 checks dependencies against OSV.dev.
  • Eval dataset scanning — Which eval dataset files the static pattern analyzers skip.
  • MCP least-privilege analysis (LP1–LP4) and MCP tool-poisoning detection (TP1–TP4) — Design notes for the MCP analyzers.

Features

  • Multi-format input: Scan Git repos, URLs, zip files, directories, or single files
  • 71 vulnerability patterns across 17 categories: prompt injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, supply chain, excessive agency, output handling, system prompt leakage, memory poisoning, tool misuse, rogue agent, anti-refusal, trigger abuse, dangerous code (AST), taint tracking, YARA signatures, MCP least privilege, and MCP tool poisoning
  • Two-stage analysis: Fast static analysis + optional LLM semantic evaluation
  • Live vulnerability lookups: SC4 queries OSV.dev for real-time CVE data with optional local snapshots and a built-in fallback
  • Multiple output formats: Terminal, JSON, Markdown, and SARIF reports
  • Risk scoring: 0-100 score with severity labels and clear recommendations
  • Baseline / false-positive suppression: Accept known findings via a glob-rule or fingerprint baseline so re-scans surface only new issues (docs)

Quick Start

Installation

Open-source software notice: This project will download and install additional third-party open source software projects. Review the license terms of these open source projects before use.

Use Python 3.12 or 3.13 for installation with prebuilt YARA wheels on supported platforms. The examples below select 3.13 explicitly; see the Python installation notes for newer interpreters. For source installs, create and activate a virtual environment first (all make targets assume the venv is active). Use uv or pip; the Makefile uses uv if available, otherwise pip.

Once a release is available on PyPI, install or upgrade SkillSpector from a Python virtual environment:

python -m pip install --upgrade skillspector
# To include the optional MCP server:
python -m pip install --upgrade 'skillspector[mcp]'

Verify the installation with skillspector --version. The GitHub installation below works ahead of the first PyPI release and for users following development.

Quick install with uv (CLI-only):

uv tool install --python 3.13 git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git
# Update later: uv tool update skillspector

If you plan to run skillspector mcp, install the MCP extra at install time:

uv tool install --python 3.13 'skillspector[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git'

From source:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git
cd skillspector

# Create and activate virtual environment
uv venv --python 3.13 .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
# or: python3.13 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

# Install for production use
make install

To contribute, follow the Development setup for a supported Python interpreter and development dependencies.

Python installation notes

The package declares Python >=3.12,<3.16 in pyproject.toml. That range does not guarantee prebuilt wheels for every dependency and platform. yara-python 4.5.4 on PyPI provides CPython 3.12/3.13 wheels, but no CPython 3.14/3.15 wheels. Installing it on those newer interpreters requires a native source build with a C toolchain and Python development headers. Such builds can fail with OpenSSL 4 headers; issue #1008 tracks that installation problem and upstream wheel availability.

If installation fails while compiling YARA, select Python 3.12 or 3.13 explicitly using the commands above. For a new CLI-only installation with pipx, first install Python 3.13 and make python3.13 available on PATH, then run:

pipx install --python python3.13 git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git

The upstream wheel-build update is separate from publishing a new release to PyPI. Check the published files before choosing a newer interpreter; a source build may still be required.

Docker (no Python required)

Run SkillSpector without installing Python by building it locally from the included Dockerfile. The image is based on the Docker Official Python 3.12-slim-bookworm image.

Build the image:

make docker-build
# or: docker build -t skillspector .

Scan a local directory by mounting your current directory into /scan, the container's working directory:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/scan" skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm

Scan with LLM analysis by passing credentials with a local .env file:

cat > .env <<'EOF'
SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
EOF

docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD:/scan" \
  --env-file .env \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/

Or pass credentials directly from your shell environment:

docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD:/scan" \
  -e SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/

Write a report to the host filesystem by writing to the mounted directory:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/scan" \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm --format json --output report.json

Optional alias for repeated static scans:

alias skillspector-docker='docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/scan" skillspector'
skillspector-docker scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm

Basic Usage

# Scan a local skill directory
skillspector scan ./my-skill/

# Scan a single SKILL.md file
skillspector scan ./SKILL.md

# Scan a Git repository
skillspector scan https://github.com/user/my-skill

# Scan a zip file
skillspector scan ./my-skill.zip

Size limits

SkillSpector enforces two independent caps on remote and archive inputs to bound the impact of oversized downloads and zip bombs:

  • Per-ingest cap: INGEST_MAX_BYTES (100 MiB) — applied to streamed URL downloads, total uncompressed size of zip archives, and post-clone disk usage of Git repos.
  • Zip member cap: INGEST_MAX_ZIP_MEMBERS (10,000) — caps the number of entries in a single zip.

Note that the per-file 1 MB analysis cap (MAX_FILE_BYTES) is a separate, downstream limit: it bounds what individual analyzers will read out of an already-ingested directory. The ingest caps above bound how much content can land on disk in the first place. A breach of either ingest cap fails closed with an IngestLimitExceededError.

Output Formats

# Terminal output (default) - pretty formatted
skillspector scan ./my-skill/

# JSON output - machine readable
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format json --output report.json

# Markdown output - for documentation
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format markdown --output report.md

# SARIF output - for CI/CD integration and IDE tooling
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format sarif --output report.sarif

Recursive Collection Scanning

Use --recursive to scan a local collection's immediate child directories as independent skills. A child can contain SKILL.md, skill.md, or a supported AISOP/AISP bundle, such as .aisop/workflow.aisop.json.

If the scan root itself contains SKILL.md or skill.md, SkillSpector scans that root as one skill. To scan children independently, point the command at a collection root without a Markdown skill manifest. Recursive output combines the child results in one report.

The default aggregate limit is 32 skills. To raise or lower it:

skillspector scan ./my-skills/ --recursive --max-skills 100 --no-llm --format json

--max-skills requires a local recursive collection and a positive integer; 0 does not mean unlimited. Discovery, byte, finding-record, time and report-size budgets still apply, so increasing the count does not guarantee complete coverage. When the count limit is reached, the CLI names the limit and suggests adjusting it or scanning sub-skills separately. The aggregate report records the omission count and reason, and coverage stays incomplete. Use --fail-on-incomplete in CI to fail on incomplete coverage.

Batch Scanning

Scan entire directories of skills in parallel from contrib/batch_scan/:

python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --no-llm
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --workers 20 -f json -o report.json
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./tests/fixtures/ -f terminal --workers 20

Supports multilingual detection (zh/ja/ko) and terminal/JSON/Markdown output.

For LLM scans with higher concurrency, configure multiple API keys following .env.example — the pool improves throughput and resilience, provided the keys don't share an account-level rate limit.

See the contrib guide for details.

Note on LLM support: The default configuration targets DeepSeek as the cheapest public option. DeepSeek-Chat is expected to sunset, and the contributor does not have hardware to test against local models. The batch scanner was originally tested with OpenAI-compatible endpoints — DeepSeek's lack of structured-output support required manual JSON-parsing patches. If you can contribute a more universal backend (Ollama, vLLM, or a different provider), PRs are very welcome.

Comparing MCP Registry snapshots

A named scan fetches only that server's published versions from the official registry, then selects entries marked as latest. If none are marked as latest, all matching versions are assessed. The server name remains the report source:

skillspector scan 'ac.inference.sh/mcp' --mcp-registry --format json --output current.json

Use https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0.1/servers as the input to scan the full catalog. Named lookups also use this stable API. The exact legacy URL https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/servers remains supported. Other URLs, including URLs with queries or fragments, are rejected. Local registry captures are supported as UTF-8 JSON, with or without a leading UTF-8 byte-order mark (BOM). The same encoding is accepted for saved Registry reports used with --mcp-registry-compare.

Start with raw registry payload captures (registry-before.json and registry-after.json). Save a scan report as previous.json, then compare a later scan against that generated local report:

skillspector scan registry-before.json --mcp-registry --format json --output previous.json
skillspector scan registry-after.json --mcp-registry --format json \
  --mcp-registry-compare previous.json --output compared.json

The optional comparison object lists added and removed server identities, changed normalized fields with their previous and current values, and an unchanged_count. Identity is the server name and version, so a new version appears as an addition and the old version as a removal if it is absent from the new scan. Acquisition source and scan timestamp are excluded from comparison. unmodeled_changes lists same-identity records whose raw-record hash changed while normalized fields match; these are not counted as unchanged. This can indicate a change to fields outside the snapshot model, or array reordering in the raw record. Package and remote ordering alone is not a normalized field change. Entries in changed may also contain changes outside the snapshot model; inspect the raw record to see those changes. Compare reports with the same selection scope: a server absent from the current input is reported as removed, which does not prove it was removed from a registry.

The comparison file must be a local report produced by this registry mode with valid normalized snapshots. Malformed, oversized or duplicate server identities are rejected. This option requires --mcp-registry and is separate from the finding-suppression --baseline: it never suppresses findings or changes risk scores, and it does not fetch or execute listed server endpoints.

Registry mode rejects skill-only controls such as --use-shipped-baseline, --transitive, --transitive-depth, --transitive-allow-prefix, and --transitive-deny-prefix with exit code 2, including an explicitly supplied default depth (--transitive-depth 1). Omit these options for registry scans.

Suppressing False Positives (baseline)

Suppress known/accepted findings so the risk score reflects only un-triaged issues and re-scans surface only new findings. See the suppression guide for the full reference.

# Accept all current findings into a baseline (run once), then commit it.
skillspector baseline ./my-skill/ -o .skillspector-baseline.yaml

# Scan against the baseline — only NEW findings are reported and scored.
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --baseline .skillspector-baseline.yaml

# Review what was suppressed (still excluded from the score).
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --baseline .skillspector-baseline.yaml --show-suppressed

A baseline can also use drift-tolerant glob rules (by rule id, file path, or message) — see .skillspector-baseline.example.yaml. Exact fingerprint baselines are evidence-bound: changing the scanned source or SkillSpector version keeps the finding active until it is reviewed again. When a selected baseline or baseline output is stored inside the skill directory, SkillSpector excludes that exact file from content analysis so its suppression text cannot create findings or enter regenerated fingerprints; sibling files remain in normal scan scope.

Explicit scan scope

For a local directory containing one SKILL.md or skill.md, repeat --exclude to omit selected files before content analysis:

skillspector scan ./my-skill --exclude 'tests/*' --exclude 'fixtures/*.json'

Patterns are case-sensitive globs matched against the entire relative POSIX path; * also matches /. Quote patterns so your shell does not expand them. This is an explicit caller option, not an author-controlled ignore file. Patterns matching either manifest name (SKILL.md or skill.md) are rejected, as are recursive, multi-skill, transitive, registry, and non-directory inputs. No-match patterns are still recorded in the report.

Files already outside the scan inventory, such as policy-excluded dependencies, retain their existing policy handling and are not counted as caller exclusions. Explicitly excluded inventory files remain in the coverage denominator as entirely uninspected. The report lists the applied patterns, excluded count and individual skipped paths; any matched exclusion makes coverage partial and prevents a SAFE recommendation. Use --fail-on-incomplete when partial scope should fail CI. These exclusions do not suppress findings in included files or override existing safety limits.

LLM Analysis

For the best results, configure an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint for semantic analysis. Pick a provider with SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER; hosted providers ship bundled default models, while CLI providers fall back to the local runtime's default model unless SKILLSPECTOR_MODEL is set. SkillSpector also works against local OpenAI-compatible servers (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp) and managed inference gateways.

Provider (SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER) Credential env var Endpoint Default model
openai OPENAI_API_KEY (+ optional OPENAI_BASE_URL) api.openai.com (or any OpenAI-compatible URL) gpt-5.4
anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY api.anthropic.com claude-opus-4-6 (meta_analyzer: claude-sonnet-4-6)
anthropic_proxy ANTHROPIC_PROXY_API_KEY + ANTHROPIC_PROXY_ENDPOINT_URL Any Vertex-style raw-predict proxy claude-sonnet-4-6
minimax MINIMAX_API_KEY (+ optional MINIMAX_REGION) Global or China regional endpoint MiniMax-M3.1-Flash
bedrock AWS_PROFILE (optional) + AWS_REGION — SigV4 via boto3 AWS Bedrock Runtime us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6
nv_build NVIDIA_INFERENCE_KEY build.nvidia.com z-ai/glm-5.3-flash
gemini GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT (+ optional GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION) via ADC Google Cloud OpenAI-compatible Gemini endpoint gemini-3.8-flash
ollama (none) OLLAMA_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:11434/v1) llama3.1:8b
azure_openai AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY + AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT Azure OpenAI Service gpt-4o (deployment defaults to the model label)
openai_compatible SKILLSPECTOR_COMPAT_API_KEY + SKILLSPECTOR_COMPAT_BASE_URL Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint llama-3.1-70b-versatile
claude_cli (none — uses local CLI auth) local claude binary local Claude runtime fallback, or SKILLSPECTOR_MODEL
codex_cli Disabled Registered for compatibility; its read-only sandbox permits host-file reads Use an HTTP API provider or another supported CLI provider
gemini_cli (none — uses local CLI auth) local gemini binary local Gemini runtime fallback, or SKILLSPECTOR_MODEL
opencode_cli (none — uses local CLI auth) local opencode (verified 1.18.31–1.18.35, 1.19.0–1.19.4) binary local OpenCode runtime fallback, or SKILLSPECTOR_MODEL

For openai_compatible gateways requiring extra HTTP headers, set SKILLSPECTOR_COMPAT_HEADERS='{"X-Tenant-ID":"my-tenant","X-API-Key":"gateway-key"}'. It must be a JSON object with string keys and values and applies to sync and async requests. Unset or blank values add no headers; invalid configuration is rejected without exposing header values. Treat this environment variable as a secret when it contains gateway API keys.

gpt-6.1-sol, claude-opus-5-5, and claude-sonnet-5-5 remain opt-in through SKILLSPECTOR_MODEL or per-slot overrides. Promoting them to defaults requires live scanner acceptance covering benign input, credential disclosure, prompt injection, refusals, and incomplete responses. Record findings, completion status, latency, and usage, and compare against previous defaults where accessible.

For NVIDIA Build's z-ai/glm-5.3-flash, SkillSpector requests high reasoning effort. Set SKILLSPECTOR_REASONING_EFFORT to override it with low, high, or max. The bundled 128,000-token context and 32,000-token output budgets are conservative application limits; they do not claim the hosted endpoint's maximum capacity.

Structured output is requested through LangChain's with_structured_output. The default is client-specific: ChatOpenAI uses json_schema, while other clients may use tool calling. Some models reject a forced tool call with HTTP 400 (tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported for this model). The anthropic and anthropic_proxy providers route those models (claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-fable-5-1, claude-mythos-5-1, or any registry entry with structured_output: json_schema) to the native JSON-schema response format. Bedrock has no JSON-schema output for them, so the bedrock provider leaves toolChoice at auto, asks for the tool call in the prompt, and retries a prose answer; it recognises the model from the model ID, a geo/global inference-profile ID, or a foundation-model / inference-profile ARN. An application-inference-profile ARN hides the model, so add that ARN to the registry (SKILLSPECTOR_MODEL_REGISTRY) with tool_choice: auto. The openai_compatible provider honours the same tool_choice: auto entry for endpoints that ignore both response_format and a forced tool_choice and answer in prose (for example iFlytek's spark-x2.5, which is bundled). The anthropic, anthropic_proxy, openai, and openai_compatible providers also recognise those Claude models inside gateway model IDs such as anthropic/claude-opus-5-5 or aws/anthropic/bedrock-claude-opus-5-5. Some OpenAI-compatible gateways turn a json_schema response format for Claude into a forced tool call, so the openai and openai_compatible providers bind the schema as a tool with tool_choice left at auto and retry a prose answer. SKILLSPECTOR_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_METHOD=json_schema|function_calling overrides the method for any provider. The method precedence is SKILLSPECTOR_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_METHOD, the provider's method hint, an analyzer preference, then the client default. TP4 prefers function_calling only for provider openai and the exact model label azure/anthropic/claude-opus-5, with reasoning/thinking controls unset; dated or suffixed labels and other providers keep their existing behavior. An explicit environment override or provider hint still wins when reasoning is configured.

MCP Server

Run SkillSpector as a Model Context Protocol server so local MCP-capable agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI) can call scanning as a tool and gate skill/MCP installs on the result — turning SkillSpector into a runtime guardrail instead of an out-of-band audit step.

skillspector mcp requires skillspector[mcp].

# Install, or reinstall if you already used the CLI-only path
uv tool install --python 3.13 --force 'skillspector[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git'

# FastMCP stdio transport for local CLI agents
skillspector mcp

# Streamable HTTP transport on a local loopback interface
skillspector mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000

The stdio transport is the current FastMCP path for local CLI agents, and the initialize hang reported in issue #199 still applies there.

The server exposes a single tool:

  • scan_skill(target, use_llm=true, output_format="json", include_report=true) — scans a Git URL, file URL, .zip, .md file, or directory and returns a structured verdict: risk_score (0-100), severity, recommendation, safe_to_install, and findings. It also reports llm_used / scan_mode so a low score from a static-only scan is never mistaken for a clean full scan.

Set include_report=false when you only need the structured verdict. This omits the rendered report string and retains every other response field, including all findings and their occurrences, analysis completeness, and LLM accounting. The default still includes the full report. Report-only details, such as components, skill metadata, and suppressed findings, are unavailable in the compact response. Scanning and report generation still run normally; output_format must remain one of json, markdown, sarif, or terminal.

Register it with Claude Code via:

claude mcp add skillspector -- skillspector mcp

Security — HTTP transport trust model

The HTTP transport ships without authentication. Any caller that can reach the port can invoke scan_skill. HTTP bindings are restricted to loopback IPs (127.0.0.1 or ::1); localhost binds to 127.0.0.1 without DNS resolution. Wildcard, routable and other hostname bindings are rejected.

  • For remote access, put an authenticating reverse proxy (e.g. nginx + mTLS) in front of the loopback listener.
  • Local paths and file:// URLs are automatically rejected over HTTP to prevent unauthenticated callers from reading arbitrary host files.

HTTP scans accept only credential-free https:// targets on allowed hosts. Targets include public Git repositories, ZIP archives, and direct file URLs such as a raw SKILL.md. These scan_skill arguments scan a public Markdown file with static analysis:

{
  "target": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/SkillSpector/main/tests/fixtures/safe_skill/SKILL.md",
  "use_llm": false
}

Git scans never use the server's Git login or Git config. If a proxy or custom CA is needed, set HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY or GIT_SSL_CAINFO in the server environment. Use stdio or the CLI for private repositories. Git redirects are rejected; use the current repository URL after a rename or transfer.

Vulnerability Patterns

SkillSpector detects 71 vulnerability patterns across 17 categories:

Prompt Injection (6 patterns)

ID Pattern Severity Description
P1 Instruction Override HIGH Commands to ignore safety constraints
P2 Hidden Instructions HIGH Malicious directives in comments/invisible text
P3 Exfiltration Commands HIGH Instructions to transmit context externally
P4 Behavior Manipulation MEDIUM Subtle instructions altering agent decisions
P5 Harmful Content CRITICAL Instructions that could cause physical harm
P9 Whitespace Padding MEDIUM Large whitespace padding hiding instructions below/beside the visible area

Anti-Refusal (3 patterns)

ID Pattern Severity Description
AR1 Refusal Suppression HIGH Instructions to never refuse or always comply (e.g. "never refuse", "always comply")
AR2 Disclaimer Suppression HIGH Instructions to omit warnings, disclaimers, or ethical commentary (e.g. "no disclaimers", "do not moralize")
AR3 Safety Policy Nullification HIGH Jailbreak framing that nullifies guardrails (e.g. "you have no restrictions", "ignore your guidelines", "do anything now")

Data Exfiltration (5 patterns)

ID Pattern Severity Description
E1 External Transmission MEDIUM Sending data to external URLs
E2 Env Variable Harvesting HIGH Enumerating, copying, or searching environment data to collect secrets. A copy traced only to a child process's env= is reported LOW
E3 File System Enumeration MEDIUM Scanning directories for sensitive files
E4 Context Leakage HIGH Transmitting conversation context externally
E5 Cloud Storage Exfiltration MEDIUM Uploading data through cloud storage SDKs or CLIs

Within bounded, fully observed context, E5 distinguishes literal AWS/GCS downloads from uploads. Simple remote-to-local cp, AWS sync, and gsutil rsync commands do not produce E5 findings. Moves, deletion options, unknown flags, dynamic operands, streams and compound shell commands retain conservative findings. This direction check does not change SDK upload detection or the CLI's exit-code policy. Direction proofs require the complete preceding context to fit within 4,096 characters. Only blank/comment lines, literal set flags (-e, -u, -f, and -o pipefail), and simple directory changes may precede a proved download. Other setup, including sourcing, autoloading, variable assignments, and earlier transfers, retains the original finding. Relative destinations after directory changes remain unproved; literal absolute file destinations are still eligible.

PE1 Excessive Permissions LOW Requesting access beyond stated functionality
PE2 Sudo/Root Execution MEDIUM Invoking elevated system privileges

Risk Scoring

Score Calculation

Each skill's score uses active findings after baseline suppression. Each active finding starts with base points for its severity.

  • CRITICAL: 50 points
  • HIGH: 25 points
  • MEDIUM: 10 points
  • LOW: 5 points

The score scales each contribution by the finding's confidence, bounded between 0 and 1. Within each rule ID, findings with positive confidence are scored in descending severity order. The first three count at full, half, and quarter weight. Further findings with the same rule ID can still appear in the report without adding points.

A 1.3× multiplier applies to a finding when its file is an executable component. The total is rounded down and capped at 100. Some conditions, such as an unapproved exclusion of executable content, impose a minimum score.

In a single-skill JSON report, risk_assessment.severity is the band for the aggregate risk_assessment.score. risk_assessment.max_issue_severity is the highest severity in the report's issues list, or NONE when that list is empty. For example, a report with one HIGH finding at 0.4 confidence in Markdown can show a score of 10, an aggregate severity of LOW, and a maximum issue severity of HIGH.

Check scan completeness when using a report to make an installation decision.

Severity Levels

Score Severity Base Recommendation
0-20 LOW SAFE
21-50 MEDIUM CAUTION
51-80 HIGH DO NOT INSTALL
81-100 CRITICAL DO NOT INSTALL

An incomplete or degraded scan can change a base recommendation of SAFE to CAUTION while keeping the score and severity.
